newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Cohen questions push for broad nato expanision.
newsitem.headline: Cohen questions push for broad nato expanision.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Wednesday night voiced strong opposition to a push by some NATO allies for quick admission of five east European countries instead of only three to membership in the alliance.

"Smaller would be better initially from my perspective," Cohen told reporters when asked whether Romania and Slovenia should be invited to join in addition to favoured candidates Poland, Hungary and Czech Republic at a July 7-8 North Atlantic Treaty Organisation summit in Madrid.

"But that's just my personal viewpoint. It has not been decided yet and ultimately the president (Bill Clinton) is going to make the decision," he added in an interview aboard his aircraft en route to Brussels from Washington for a two-day NATO defence ministers meeting.

A push by France and several other allies for Romania and Slovenia to be invited immediately along with the three leading candidates will be a major topic of discussion at the ministerial meeting on Thursday and Friday in Brussels.
Those alliance members say that Slovenia's location in the Balkans and Romania's Black Sea coast make them important in two of Europe's most volatile regions.
"Obviously, there is support on the part of the Europeans for Romania and Slovenia," said Cohen.
But he cited the high cost of enlargement, problems over the ability of some new states to meet alliance military obligations and some U.S. Senate mistrust of broadening NATO at all.
"We want to make sure that we hold the cohesiveness of NATO together," he said.

Instead, Cohen said, western leaders meeting in Madrid next month should make clear to states seeking to join that they could become members later by holding to a democratic course and by pressing for a military integration with the alliance.
"It's an open door and we want to make sure that we emphasise very strongly that those who don't come in...in the next round could gain accession."

Clinton met in Washington on Wednesday with senior senators to discuss NATO expansion and Cohen pointed out that some in the senate, including Republican John Warner of Virginia, have voiced strong reservations about enlargement at high cost to current members.
"No matter what happens in Madrid, the next step is to persuade the Senate to ratify it," Cohen said. The parliaments of other NATO countries must ratify any expansion.
On another key NATO issue, Cohen said that the United States hoped that France would follow through on its indications last year that it might rejoin the NATO military structure after decades.
But that move has been held up by a major dispute between Paris and Washington over U.S. command of NATO's southern military flank.

"I would hope that the French would consider integrating fully with NATO. I think it's important for them. I think it's important for NATO itself, but I don't know what their position is going to be in view of the (French general) election," he said.

Cohen told reporters that talks on France's demand to turn the southern flank over to a European commander and on NATO military integration had apparently been put on hold by the recent French election.
